title: Odd Even Jump
description: Brute force to optimized: simulating the full jump sequence per start versus precomputed next-jump targets (sort + monotonic stack) combined with backward DP.

blocks.text: You are given an integer array arr. From a starting index, you may make a series of jumps. Odd-numbered jumps (1st, 3rd, 5th, ...) must land on the SMALLEST value that is >= the current value, choosing the smallest index in case of ties. Even-numbered jumps (2nd, 4th, 6th, ...) must land on the LARGEST value that is <= the current value, choosing the smallest index in case of ties. A starting index is "good" if, starting there, you can reach the last index (via any number of jumps, alternating odd and even). Return the number of good starting indices.

blocks.caption: Precomputing every index's "next odd jump" and "next even jump" target via sorting plus a monotonic stack, then a backward DP, avoids re-simulating every start individually

{"headers":["Signal in the problem","Pattern it points to"],"rows":[["\"Next SMALLEST value >= x\" and \"next LARGEST value <= x\" are exactly next-greater/next-smaller style queries","These can each be resolved with a monotonic stack technique, ONCE the indices are considered in the right VALUE order (not array order)"],["Whether a start is \"good\" depends on whether the position it jumps TO is ALSO good (for the opposite jump type)","A backward dynamic programming pass, computing reachability from the END of the array toward the start, since each position's answer depends on a LATER position's answer"]]}

blocks.text: Two different "next" relationships need to be precomputed for every index: where would an ODD jump from here land, and where would an EVEN jump from here land. Once those are known for every index, whether a start is "good" becomes a straightforward dependency: index i (via an odd jump) is good if and only if the odd-jump target is good FOR AN EVEN JUMP, and vice versa.

blocks.title: Analogy: A Board Game With Alternating Move Rules
blocks.text: Imagine a board game where on ODD turns, a piece must move to the space with the SMALLEST value that is at least as large as its current space (closest match going up), and on EVEN turns, to the space with the LARGEST value that is at most its current space (closest match going down), always breaking ties toward the earliest such space. Winning means reaching the final space, using any sequence of alternating odd/even moves; this problem asks how many starting spaces let a player eventually win.

blocks.caption: Sorting indices by value (ascending for odd, descending for even) turns "next greater/smaller" into a monotonic-stack-solvable next-index problem

blocks.text: Before simulating the ENTIRE jump sequence separately for every possible starting index (redundant, since many starts share overlapping jump chains), notice that precomputing each index's single "next odd jump" and "next even jump" target ONCE, then using dynamic programming, answers every starting index's reachability simultaneously.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: "Smallest value >= arr[i], among positions AFTER i" is a variant of "next greater or equal element," and "largest value <= arr[i]" is the mirror "next smaller or equal element": both are classic monotonic-stack-solvable queries, but INDEXED BY VALUE rather than by array position.

Observation 2: Sorting indices by VALUE (ascending, with index as a tiebreaker, for the odd-jump query; descending for the even-jump query) and then applying a monotonic stack of INDICES (checking "is there an earlier, still-unresolved index waiting for a target with a bigger index than itself") correctly computes each index's next-jump target in O(n log n) total.

Observation 3: Once every index's next-odd-jump and next-even-jump targets are known, "is index i good starting with an odd jump" reduces to "does the odd-jump target REACH THE END starting with an even jump," a simple lookup, IF that later index's answer is already known.

Observation 4: Processing indices from the LAST one backward to the FIRST guarantees that whenever position i's answer is being computed, whatever LATER position it might jump to has its answer ALREADY computed, making a single backward pass sufficient.
This is a two-part technique: precompute next-jump targets via sorting plus a monotonic stack, then resolve reachability for every index with a single backward dynamic programming pass.

For each possible starting index, directly simulate the entire jump sequence (alternating odd and even jumps, each computed by scanning forward for the required target), checking whether it eventually reaches the last index.

items: For each starting index, repeatedly find the correct next jump target (scanning forward each time, alternating between the odd-jump and even-jump rules) until either the last index is reached or no valid jump exists.
Count how many starting indices successfully reach the last index this way.

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: Directly simulating each start's ENTIRE jump sequence matches the problem's definition exactly, though it repeats a lot of overlapping work across different starting points.
The inner forward scan for each individual jump directly implements the "smallest >= " / "largest <=" target rules.

blocks.text: Correctly determines reachability for every starting index, since it directly simulates the exact jump rules from each one.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n^3) in the worst case: up to n starting points, each potentially needing up to n jumps, each jump requiring an O(n) forward scan.
Space: O(1) extra.

Limitation: massively redundant work is repeated across different starting indices whose jump sequences overlap; precomputing each index's next-jump targets ONCE (via a monotonic stack) and reusing them via dynamic programming reduces this to O(n log n) total.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text: The brute force re-simulates overlapping jump sequences repeatedly. Instead, precompute nextOdd[i] and nextEven[i] for EVERY index ONCE: sort indices by value (ascending for nextOdd, descending for nextEven, with index as a tiebreaker), then apply a monotonic stack of indices to find, for each index in that sorted order, the earliest STILL-PENDING smaller index it can serve as a target for. Then run a single backward DP pass: canOdd[i] and canEven[i], where the last index trivially reaches itself, and every other index's answer depends on looking up its precomputed jump target's (opposite-type) answer.

Build ascByValue and descByValue: index orderings sorted by (value, index) ascending and (-value, index) ascending respectively. For each ordering, walk through it with a monotonic stack of indices (kept in increasing index order): whenever the stack's top is SMALLER than the current index being processed, that current index becomes the target for the popped one. This computes nextOdd and nextEven. Then, starting from canOdd[n-1] = canEven[n-1] = true, walk backward: canOdd[i] = canEven[nextOdd[i]] (if nextOdd[i] exists), canEven[i] = canOdd[nextEven[i]] (if nextEven[i] exists); count every i where canOdd[i] is true (since the first jump is always odd).
Precompute next-jump targets via sorting plus a monotonic stack, then resolve reachability with a single backward dynamic programming pass.

blocks.title: Final answer
blocks.text: The backward DP correctly identifies 2 good starting indices, matching the expected result.

codes.python:
def odd_even_jumps(arr):
    n = len(arr)

    def make_next(order):                                                  # order: indices sorted by the RELEVANT criterion (value, then index)
        next_idx = [-1] * n
        stack = []                                                          # a monotonic stack of indices, kept in INCREASING index order
        for i in order:
            while stack and stack[-1] < i:                                 # i is a valid "target" for everything smaller-indexed waiting
                next_idx[stack.pop()] = i
            stack.append(i)
        return next_idx

    asc_by_value = sorted(range(n), key=lambda i: (arr[i], i))             # for "next odd jump": smallest arr[j] >= arr[i]
    desc_by_value = sorted(range(n), key=lambda i: (-arr[i], i))           # for "next even jump": largest arr[j] <= arr[i]
    next_odd = make_next(asc_by_value)
    next_even = make_next(desc_by_value)

    can_odd = [False] * n
    can_even = [False] * n
    can_odd[n - 1] = can_even[n - 1] = True                                # the last index trivially "reaches itself" with 0 jumps
    good = 1
    for i in range(n - 2, -1, -1):                                         # walk BACKWARD: whether i is good depends on later indices
        if next_odd[i] != -1:
            can_odd[i] = can_even[next_odd[i]]                             # an odd jump from i must be followed by a REACHABLE even-jump position
        if next_even[i] != -1:
            can_even[i] = can_odd[next_even[i]]                            # an even jump from i must be followed by a REACHABLE odd-jump position
        if can_odd[i]:                                                     # the FIRST jump from any start is always odd-numbered
            good += 1
    return good


if __name__ == "__main__":
    print(odd_even_jumps([10, 13, 12, 14, 15]))

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n log n), dominated by the two sorts; the monotonic stack passes and DP are each O(n).
Space: O(n), for the sorted orderings, next-jump arrays, and DP arrays.

Sorting indices by value transforms "find the next index (by ARRAY position) with the smallest value >= mine" into a problem solvable by a monotonic stack: processing indices in increasing VALUE order, an index i can serve as the target for any SMALLER-array-position index still waiting on the stack, since i is the smallest qualifying value encountered so far in this value-order traversal. The backward DP then correctly composes these single-jump results into full multi-jump reachability, since a start is good if and only if its immediate jump target is ALSO good for the opposite jump type, all the way down to the trivially-good last index.

items: The tiebreak (using index as a secondary sort key) correctly implements the problem's "choose the smallest such index" rule for ties in value.
The monotonic stack in makeNext specifically stays in INCREASING index order, since it is answering "which of these earlier (smaller index), still-pending positions can I serve as the target for."
The backward DP loop's order is essential: canOdd[i] and canEven[i] can only be correctly computed once whatever LATER index they might jump to has already been resolved.

blocks.text: Problems combining a "next greater/smaller by VALUE" query with multi-step reachability can be decomposed into two independent, well-known techniques: sorting plus a monotonic stack for the value-based next-index queries, and backward dynamic programming for composing single-step results into full reachability.

items: Forgetting the tiebreak rule (smallest index among equal values), which changes which index is actually the target.
Running the DP FORWARD instead of BACKWARD, which would try to use not-yet-computed values for later indices.
Confusing which sort order (ascending vs. descending) corresponds to odd jumps versus even jumps.

items: Explicitly separating this problem into its TWO independent sub-techniques (value-sorted monotonic stack for next-jump targets, and backward DP for reachability) up front makes an otherwise intimidating "hard" problem much more approachable to explain and implement.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: "Next greater/smaller value (not next greater INDEX)" combined with "reachability through alternating rules" points toward sorting-by-value plus a monotonic stack, followed by backward dynamic programming.

items: Why does the monotonic stack for next-jump computation need to process indices in VALUE order rather than array order? Because the "next greater/smaller VALUE" relationship is fundamentally about value comparisons, not positional adjacency, so processing by value order lets the standard next-greater-element stack logic apply correctly.

How would you extend this to THREE alternating jump types instead of two? Three separate next-jump arrays and three DP arrays (canType1, canType2, canType3) would be needed, with the recurrence extended accordingly.

What is the role of the tiebreak (index ascending) in the sort comparator? It ensures that among multiple indices sharing the same value, the algorithm consistently resolves to the SMALLEST such index, exactly matching the problem's stated tie-breaking rule.

A sophisticated combination of the monotonic stack "next greater/smaller element" pattern (applied here to VALUE-sorted order rather than array order) with backward dynamic programming, building on the simpler monotonic stack techniques from Next Greater Element I and Daily Temperatures elsewhere in this category.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text:
Brute force: O(n^3) time, O(1) space.
Optimized (sort + monotonic stack + backward DP): O(n log n) time, O(n) space.

items: Pattern: Value-sorted monotonic stack for next-jump targets, combined with backward dynamic programming
Core Idea: Precompute every index's single next-odd-jump and next-even-jump target (via sorting by value plus a monotonic stack), then resolve full multi-jump reachability with one backward DP pass
Time: O(n log n)
Space: O(n)

Most Important Observation: Sorting indices by VALUE (not array position) turns the value-based "next greater/smaller" query into a monotonic-stack-solvable problem, exactly like the classic technique, just reordered
Interview Difficulty: Hard
One-line memory trick: Sort by value, monotonic stack finds next-jump targets; DP backward: canOdd[i]=canEven[nextOdd[i]], canEven[i]=canOdd[nextEven[i]]
